newsitem.title: USA: INSIGHT - Dollar's fate tied to U.S. stocks, bonds.
newsitem.headline: INSIGHT - Dollar's fate tied to U.S. stocks, bonds.

text.p: A marked selloff on Wednesday left the dollar down on its luck but not necessarily down on its knees as analysts expected its fate to be tied to the near-term performance of U.S. financial assets.
"Bonds and stocks led the way," one currency trader said. "It's unclear what's going to happen next, and how this will affect the dollar."

The 30-year Treasury benchmark bond ended down 1-26/32 to yield 6.63 percent -- its highest closing level since November 6. The Dow industrials ended down 70.73 points at 6402.52 after losing nearly 130 points earlier in the day.

The dollar, after displaying weakness mostly since Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's remarks about equities overvaluation last Thursday, remained vulnerable to global investors' mood swings, analysts said.
Traders said they expected the selling pressure to remain through Asia trading and spill over into the European session due to the lack of bargain-hunters in the 1.5350 area.
Al Inglesino, technical analyst at MCM CurrencyWatch, predicted that unless the dollar "climbs back above 1.5425 marks, we're looking to return lower to the 1.5290/70 area."
"The near-term trend is lower," Inglesino forecast.
The dollar/yen outlook seemed somewhat brighter, provided 112.55 -- or the 62-percent retracement of the upward move to the recent high at 113.70 -- holds.
"If we lose 112.55, the risks are rising of a return to 111.80," Inglesino said.
Looking at the upside, technical analysts said dollar/yen needs to take out a strong resistance level in the 113.60/70 area before an attack on an objective at 114.75 yen can be considered.
Inglesino also described dollar/Swiss as "pretty much a mirror image in the last day or two of dollar/mark."
Dollar/Swiss, often a good indicator of overall trend, appeared ready to test key support at 1.3070, a level that, if lost, would point to a fall to 1.2915, Inglesino also said.
"There is a bearish tone in all the studies. It looks like we are going to revisit the lower end of that range from where a recovery might take root," Inglesino added.

Already on Tuesday, analysts had warned a sharp correction in U.S. equities, particularly if accompanied by pressure on Treasury bonds, could lead investors to get out of U.S. financial assets and thus sell the dollar.
